title: Beyond the mean: A statistical re‐evaluation of construction and demolition waste in dry‐cast paving blocks reveals no interior optimum and overstated standard compliance
content:
Abstract

Dry-cast (zero-slump) concrete paving blocks are a potential application for recycled construction and demolition (C&D) materials, but identifying a replacement “optimum” from small-sample means can confuse a sample-specific maximum with a reproducible engineering optimum. Using specimen-level data from a single-plant case study of granitic pavers containing recycled concrete aggregate (RCA), waste gypsum, or tannery sludge as stone-dust replacements, this study re-evaluates strength inference, standard-based acceptance, and multi-objective screening. Across the tested RCA levels (30%–60%), ANOVA detected an overall difference driven by the reference mixture, whereas post-hoc comparisons did not resolve statistically significant differences among the recycled mixtures. A bootstrap ranking identified RCA40 as the most frequently weakest mixture; it did not establish a stable interior optimum. Applying the characteristic-strength calculation used in this study, rather than relying on mean strength alone, classified RCA40 and G20 below the 35 MPa criterion despite their means exceeding 35 MPa. The Derringer–Suich score and the cost–characteristic-strength Pareto analysis produced different selections because they used different objectives, candidate sets, and aggregation rules. RCA60 remains a candidate for further validation, not a fully qualified industrial recommendation, because its absorption and abrasion results are unavailable. The principal contribution is a transparent, variance-aware re-analysis that separates evidence of statistical differences from engineering acceptance and makes the limits of small-sample inference explicit. This work is relevant to manufacturers of concrete paving blocks and C&D waste recyclers seeking to increase recycled-material use without relying on mean strength alone. The analysis shows how within-mixture variability can change an apparent acceptance decision. Because durability measurements are incomplete for RCA60 and the study covers one production plant with four to five specimens per mixture, the results provide a screening framework and a preliminary experimental target rather than a validated industrial operating window. The estimated unit-cost reduction of about 15% is specific to the cost data in this case study and should not be assumed to transfer unchanged to other plants or feedstocks. This study contributes a specimen-level statistical re-evaluation of the commonly reported replacement “optimum” in dry-cast pavers. It distinguishes a lack of statistically significant differences among tested RCA levels from proof that no optimum can exist, and it contrasts mean-based assessment with the characteristic-strength calculation applied here. It also documents why a weighted desirability score may select a different mixture from a Pareto analysis. The available evidence does not validate RCA60 for all durability criteria; therefore, the study frames the upper replacement level as a candidate for additional testing, not as a definitive industrial optimum.
